extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers and performers (stand‑up, sitcom/TV writers, joke writers)
extracted.subtask_short: using rule of three in comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on writing jokes using the comedic Rule of Threes: how to set up the pattern, craft the punchline/turn, avoid common traps, and adapt variations. Targeted guidance for writers and performers creating short jokes, lines, or lists-of-three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-Threes principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule-of-Threes establishes a pattern and then ends with something unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set two (or more) items to build a recognizable pattern, then deliver a third item that breaks expectation. The break should create the laugh by subverting the established rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number needed to establish pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually two items are sufficient to establish the pattern. Three is overkill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can get the pattern with two items; audiences are conditioned to the rhythm of threes so adding more can feel wrong. Avoid long enumerations (four or more) that ruin the rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of setup pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: You must be very careful that the two first items clearly establishes the pattern you’re setting up. You don’t want the audience to have to work to make the connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the category or relationship of the first items obvious so the punchline can play off it. Example contrast: 'The Giants, Detroit, and the Teamsters.' (unclear) vs 'The Giants, the Tigers, and the Teamsters.' (clearly baseball teams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid words or items that can be read in multiple categories (e.g., 'The Reds, the Blues, and the Teamsters' — could be political, sports teams, or drugs). Ambiguity forces the audience to work and weakens the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep setup straight; save the funny for the payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: You hurt the punchline if one of the setups is funny. It's okay that the set up be straight. Save the funny for the payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one of your setup items is itself a joke, you risk canceling the later payoff ('joke-on-a-joke'). Use a neutral, unfunny setup so the surprise third item lands harder (example: avoid 'Linda, Moon Unit, and Mother Teresa' as a setup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid convoluted setups
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t make your set up too convoluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, detailed setups make the audience 'putting in a Blu‑Ray' by the time you hit the punchline. Keep setups short and simple so attention and rhythm are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoff should subvert but still connect
rubrics_metrics.description: The payoff has to break the pattern but not so much so that it’s a non-sequitur. The punchline has to connect to the pattern. It’s not that it doesn’t belong, it’s that you don't expect it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unexpected item must relate enough to the established set to make sense while surprising the audience (example: 'The Giants, the Tigers, and poi.' — odd but ties to the list theme). Totally unrelated non-sequiturs usually fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid predictability; craft the best payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger with the Rule-of-Threes is that it’s such a familiar form that audiences see it coming. ... So extra pressure is now placed on your punchline. Try to find the best version of your payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the device is well known, spend effort iterating the payoff for freshness and surprise; don't rely on the structure alone to produce the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and precise wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The more specific in comedy the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most precise, image-creating word possible — brevity and specificity often make a line funnier. For example, a concrete single-word image can out-perform a vague concept. Also consider syllable/word economy for rhythm and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience / cultural accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: I will caution you that you need to know your audience. If you’re not Jewish you might never have heard of gefilte fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure references or 'funny words' are understood by your target audience; a funny-sounding word alone doesn't guarantee laughs for every crowd. Tailor references or provide context where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely on funny-sounding words alone
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s a fallacy that funny words alone are enough to get a laugh. They may in some cases but don’t rely it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funny-sounding words can help, but should support a clear pattern and payoff rather than substitute for a clever turn or proper setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Think rhythm, think timing. This is comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery — pacing, emphasis, and when you pause — is as important as word choice. The Rule of Threes depends on timing to establish pattern and then deliver the turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations: Stan Daniels' Turn (inverse turn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stan Daniels’ Turn: the punchline was the exact opposite of the first two. 'She’s hateful, she’s despicable, I’m in love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inversion is a recognizable formula that can work, but use with caution (author notes: 'Yes, it's formula, and it often works, but I'd avoid it.'). Treat as a tool, not a default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility of list items
rubrics_metrics.description: The list doesn't have to be objects or names. It can be words...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can apply the pattern to different units — names, objects, words, ideas — as long as the pattern is clear and the punchline subverts expectation.
